clue.text: Chapel our people attached to hospital across meadow

indicators.note: one thing laid across another spans it, so the second word sits inside the first

parts.note: a ley (or lea) is a meadow or grassland

explanation.surface: A congregation's chapel joined to a hospital on the far side of a field.
explanation.walkthrough: SAN, short for sanatorium, is a crossword staple for hospital; 'across' puts the meadow inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: A Wesleyan chapel is a Methodist place of worship, named after John Wesley, so the word serves as a noun for such a chapel.

clue.text: Heroin among goods around entrance to Victorian docks

indicators.note: a thing placed among others ends up inside them, so the drug goes in
to go around something is to enclose it, so the goods also wrap the Victorian letter
an entrance is the way in, so only the first letter of the next word is used

explanation.surface: Drugs hidden in cargo arriving at the old Victorian docks.
explanation.walkthrough: Two small pieces go into the goods at different places: the drug near the front, the Victorian letter near the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Wharves are the quays or landing stages where ships tie up to load and unload, much like docks.

clue.text: Bristly group given cards outside old university

indicators.note: something outside another surrounds it, so the cards wrap round the letters for the old university

explanation.surface: A prickly crowd of card players beyond an ancient university.
explanation.definitionFit: Setaceous is the botanist's word for bristly, from the Latin seta, a bristle.

clue.text: Fugitive starts to seek king's protection? Sounds rather like it

indicators.note: the setter says the letters spoken aloud come close to the word wanted
starts are beginnings, so only the opening letter of each following word counts

parts.note: the opening letters of these three words, said as letter names

explanation.surface: A runaway hoping for the monarch's sanctuary, which sounds like the sensible move.
explanation.walkthrough: Say the three letters ESS-KAY-PEE and you hear ESCAPEE; 'rather' admits the sound is close, not exact.
explanation.definitionFit: An escapee is someone who has broken out and is on the run, a fugitive.

clue.text: School rebel held in check by little woman

indicators.note: someone held in check is restrained inside another's grip, so the rebel goes inside the woman

parts.note: Amy March, one of the sisters in Little Women
Jack Cade led the Kentish rebellion of 1450

explanation.surface: A schoolgirl troublemaker is kept in line by a small woman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Little woman' is not just a small person: it points to Alcott's novel Little Women.
explanation.definitionFit: An academy is a school, especially a secondary or specialist one.

clue.text: Geordie mother's woeful book about warm-blooded beast

parts.note: a Geordie (from Newcastle) says mam for mum

indicators.note: turning about means facing the other way, so the book's short name is read backwards

parts.note: Lam. abbreviates Lamentations, the Old Testament book of grief

explanation.surface: A Newcastle mum's sad book about some creature.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's stands for 'has': MAM has LAM turned round after it.
explanation.definitionFit: Mammals are the warm-blooded animals that suckle their young, so the phrase is a description of the class.

clue.text: Play role madam adapted

indicators.note: an adapted text has been reworked, so these letters are put into a new order

parts.note: the nine letters taken as written

explanation.surface: An actress's part as a brothel-keeper, rewritten for the stage.
explanation.definitionFit: A melodrama is a sensational stage play with exaggerated characters, so it is one kind of play.

clue.text: Graduate has traveller put in the shade

indicators.note: the degree has something put in it, holding it inside

parts.note: a commercial traveller is a sales agent

explanation.surface: A graduate eclipsed by a travelling companion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put in the shade' looks like an idiom for outshone; the shade is a colour.
explanation.definitionFit: Magenta is a purplish-red colour, a shade named after the 1859 battle of Magenta.

clue.text: Examine stories written and reported

indicators.note: something reported is passed on by word of mouth, so the sound matters, not the spelling

parts.note: an annal is a written chronicle, and stories in the sense of fibs are lies

explanation.surface: Study the stories that were set down and those told by word of mouth.
explanation.walkthrough: Said quickly, ANNAL LIES runs together into the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To analyse is to examine something closely by breaking it into its parts.

clue.text: Plan Hecate concocted, giving access to place of worship

definitions.text: giving access to place of worship
definitions.note: the answer is a noun: the part of a college chapel that leads into it

indicators.note: a concocted scheme is cooked up, so these letters are mixed into a new order

parts.note: the ten letters taken as written

explanation.surface: The witch-goddess Hecate devises a scheme to get into a temple.
explanation.walkthrough: Hecate is the goddess of witchcraft (she appears in Macbeth), which suits a plot; here she is only letters.
explanation.definitionFit: An antechapel is the outer room at the west end of a college chapel, through which worshippers enter.

clue.text: Author of ballad opera defends right to identify poet

indicators.note: a defender stands round what it protects, so the first name encloses the letter

parts.note: John Gay wrote The Beggar's Opera, a ballad opera

explanation.surface: One writer is used to pick out another.
explanation.walkthrough: GAY with R inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Thomas Gray wrote the Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard, one of the best-known English poems.

clue.text: Politician's office quietly distancing governor's house from corruption

indicators.note: to distance two things is to put something between them, so the soft letter separates the two parts

parts.note: p (piano) is the musical mark for quiet
the official home of a colonial governor or resident

explanation.surface: A politician's job keeps a governor's mansion quietly clear of graft.
explanation.walkthrough: The order runs against the clue: corruption comes first, then the quiet letter, then the house it is kept apart from.
explanation.definitionFit: The vice-presidency is the post a deputy head of state holds, an office in politics.

clue.text: Appear early, at regular intervals, like some rain

parts.note: to show up is to appear

indicators.note: at regular intervals means every other letter is picked from the word

explanation.surface: A weather forecast: rain that turns up early and comes back now and then.
explanation.definitionFit: Showery weather brings brief falls of rain, so it describes rain that comes in bursts.

clue.text: Routine extremely suitable for setting up again

indicators.note: the extremes of a word are its two ends, so only the outer letters are kept

explanation.surface: A daily procedure that suits re-establishing something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Extremely suitable' reads as 'very apt'; 'extremely' belongs to the word before it.
explanation.definitionFit: Refitting is equipping or fitting out again, as with a ship or a shop being set up afresh.

clue.text: Old man adopting an excellent remedy for all ills

indicators.note: a family adopting a child takes it in, so the father's word takes the other words inside

explanation.surface: An old fellow takes up a marvellous cure-all.
explanation.definitionFit: A panacea is a supposed universal cure, named after the Greek goddess of healing.

clue.text: Porter about to carry article in Londonderry town

indicators.note: carrying something means holding it, so the word for about holds the article and the in

explanation.surface: A railway porter carries luggage around a town in Northern Ireland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Porter' looks like a baggage carrier; it is a songwriter's surname.
explanation.definitionFit: Coleraine is a town on the River Bann in County Londonderry, Northern Ireland.

clue.text: Dog's condition fine, after taking pig-food

indicators.note: coming after something means being placed behind it, so the food is written first

parts.note: mast is the beech nuts and acorns pigs forage on

explanation.surface: A vet's report: the dog is healthy now it has eaten.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dog's' reads as 'Dog is': the definition, then the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: The mastiff is a large, powerful breed of dog, so the word names one kind.

clue.text: Movement with neat dancing

parts.note: and joins things, as with does

indicators.note: dancing feet never stay in one place, so these letters move into a new order

explanation.surface: A tidy step in a dance routine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Movement' suggests a dancer's motion; it is part of a symphony.
explanation.definitionFit: An andante is a movement of a musical work played at a moderate walking pace.

clue.text: Hard work providing road for use ultimately in journey

indicators.note: one thing put for another stands in its place, so the road replaces that letter

parts.note: to make a journey is to travel

indicators.note: ultimately means in the end, so only the last letter of the word is meant

parts.note: the A1 is Britain's longest road, its 1 read as the letter I

explanation.surface: Toil that builds a road for travellers to use on a trip.
explanation.walkthrough: The A1 runs from London to Edinburgh; crosswords often write it as AI.
explanation.definitionFit: Travail is painful, laborious effort, an old word for toil.

clue.text: Champion with record reserves

parts.note: to back a cause is to champion it
a log is a written record

explanation.surface: A sporting champion who also holds a record, kept on the bench.
explanation.definitionFit: A backlog is a stock of work or goods held over, an accumulated reserve.

clue.text: Stole across border, beginning to invade old country

indicators.note: something lying across another covers it from side to side, so the stole wraps the edge and the letter

parts.note: a feather boa is a long scarf, like a stole
the hem is a garment's edge

indicators.note: a beginning is the start, so only the first letter of the next word is taken

explanation.surface: Someone crossed a frontier stealthily to start invading a former nation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stole' reads as the past tense of steal; it is a scarf.
explanation.definitionFit: Bohemia was a kingdom in central Europe, now the western part of the Czech Republic.

clue.text: A sound aid for those trying to find Hereford?

definitions.text: A sound aid for those trying to find Hereford?

parts.words: A sound aid for those trying to find Hereford?
parts.note: surface reading: a good guide or map for travellers heading to the English city of Hereford

parts.words: A sound aid for those trying to find Hereford?
parts.note: setter's reading: something that makes a noise to help farmers locate a Hereford, a breed of beef cattle

explanation.walkthrough: Hereford is both a cathedral city and a breed of cattle, and 'sound' means noise, not reliable.
explanation.definitionFit: A bell hung round a beast's neck clangs as it moves, so a herdsman can track it down.

clue.text: Aim to support gallery — it's a blessing

indicators.note: in a down clue a support goes underneath, so this piece is written below the other

parts.note: the gods is the highest gallery in a theatre
an end is a goal or purpose

explanation.surface: An art gallery's mission statement, read as a stroke of luck.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gallery' suggests paintings; in theatre the cheapest top seats are called the gods.
explanation.definitionFit: A godsend is something welcome that arrives just when needed, a blessing.

clue.text: Fast asleep, so late for everybody?

parts.note: the late So-and-so is someone who has died
as in 'dead to' meaning gone as far as someone is concerned

explanation.surface: Someone so deeply asleep they are late for everyone else.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Late' looks like being behind time; it means deceased, which is how deep sleep looks to everyone else.
explanation.definitionFit: Dead to the world is an idiom for being in a sleep so deep that nothing can wake you.

clue.text: Peruvian provides pad for refreshing type, we hear

indicators.note: what we hear is a word judged by its sound, not its spelling

parts.note: an inking pad re-inks printing type; in a non-rhotic accent the two words sound alike

explanation.surface: A man from Peru supplies a cushion for a tired sort of person.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Refreshing type' suggests a person who perks you up; it is printing type given fresh ink.
explanation.definitionFit: The Inca were the people whose empire ruled Peru before the Spanish conquest, so an Inca is Peruvian.

clue.text: Desert person in Leah's time, wandering around island

indicators.note: letters that wander about lose their places, and here they wrap round the extra letter as they roam

explanation.surface: A desert nomad of Old Testament days, when Leah lived, roams round an island.
explanation.walkthrough: Leah, Jacob's wife, sets the scene in Genesis, where Ishmael's descendants also live.
explanation.definitionFit: The Ishmaelites, descended from Abraham's son Ishmael, were desert-dwelling nomads in the Bible.

clue.text: Consequence of flight of black convict

parts.note: an old lag is a long-serving prisoner

explanation.surface: What happens when a dark-skinned convict escapes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flight' looks like a prisoner's escape; it is air travel.
explanation.definitionFit: Jet lag is the tiredness that follows a long flight across time zones.

clue.text: Learn about bad weather delaying husband in terminal

indicators.note: to be about something is to be around it, so the verb wraps the weather
delaying the husband's letter makes it arrive last, so it moves from the front to the end

parts.note: to read a subject is to study it

explanation.surface: Someone hears of a storm that holds up a husband stuck in an airport terminal.
explanation.walkthrough: To read a subject at university is to study it, a British usage; 'terminal' looks like an airport building, but it is where a railway line ends.
explanation.definitionFit: A railhead is the point where a railway line ends, a terminal.
